name: Congolese Moambe Chicken
description: Poulet moambe is DR Congo's national dish, and real moambe sauce - made by pounding palm nuts into a thick, rust-red cream - isn't just an ingredient in the dish, cooks and sources alike describe it AS the dish; there's no substitute that fully replicates its specific earthy creaminess and color. Peanut butter is the genuinely recognized substitute used even by Congolese cooks abroad when palm nut cream isn't available, which is what this version uses, but it's honestly a different, milder flavor than the real thing.
steps_detailed: Brown the chicken with the onion, garlic, and ginger, 8-9 minutes.
Whisk the peanut butter with the tomatoes and a little water, then add to the pot along with the jalapeño.
Simmer 25-28 minutes until the chicken is very tender.

name: Congolese Fufu
description: Fufu, cassava pounded into a smooth, stretchy dough, is one of DR Congo's most essential staple starches, traditionally torn by hand to scoop up soup or stew.
steps_detailed: Boil the cassava until completely soft, 20-25 minutes.
Drain and pound vigorously until smooth and stretchy, free of lumps.
steps: Boil the cassava until completely soft, 20-25 minutes.

name: Congolese Saka Saka
description: Saka saka (also called pondu), pounded cassava leaves simmered with peanut and palm oil, is a genuine Congolese staple - real cassava leaves aren't a distinct item here, so spinach stands in for a milder, less fibrous approximation, missing cassava leaves' real earthy density.
steps_detailed: Cook the onion 4-5 minutes.
Whisk the peanut butter with a little water, add to the pot along with the tomatoes and spinach.
Simmer 15-18 minutes until well combined and thickened.
steps: Cook the onion 4-5 minutes.

name: Congolese Liboke
description: Liboke, fish seasoned and wrapped in banana leaf to steam in its own juices, is a genuine Congolese cooking technique, the wrapping keeping the fish moist and infusing it with real aromatics.
steps_detailed: Rub the fish with the garlic and ginger.
Wrap tightly in foil with the tomatoes.
Bake at 400F (200C) for 20-22 minutes until just cooked through, sealed in its own steam.
steps: Rub the fish with the garlic and ginger.

name: Congolese Chikwangue
description: Chikwangue, fermented cassava dough wrapped in leaves and steamed, a genuine Congolese staple with a distinctive sour tang from real fermentation.
steps_detailed: Mix the grated cassava with water and let ferment at room temperature 24-48 hours.
Wrap tightly and steam over simmering water 45-50 minutes until firm.

description: Grilled meat, marinated simply with garlic and pepper, a beloved Congolese way of preparing meat for gatherings - beef stands in here for goat, a more widely available protein with a similarly hearty character.
steps_detailed: Rub the beef with the garlic and jalapeño.
Grill over medium-high heat, turning, 12-15 minutes, until well charred and cooked through.
